

# GATE 2016 CS1: Q26 (printed CS Q16)

**Question:** [Official archived paper page 8](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1popAHO-cX69oQEx_tD0wZXL1tTrBljeO/view); consult original wording, diagrams and choices.

**Type / marks:** MCQ, 1 mark(s).

**Official answer:** D

**Derived answer:** D

**Source access:** Open archive member CS/CS2016.pdf inside the linked official CS.zip. Page numbers refer to the extracted PDF, not the Drive preview.

**Paraphrased problem context:** Which language is generated by S→aS | bS | ε? A: {a^n b^m:n,m≥0}. B: All words over {a,b} with equal numbers of a and b. C: {a^n:n≥0} union {b^n:n≥0} union {a^n b^n:n≥0}. D: {a,b}*.

## Solution

At every step S can emit either a or b and recurse, then terminate with epsilon. Every finite binary-alphabet word, including epsilon, is generated, giving {a, b}*, D.

For any desired word w, choose the production beginning with its next character repeatedly, then use S→ε after its final character. For example baba follows S⇒bS⇒baS⇒babS⇒babaS⇒baba. Conversely, every production emits only a or b, so no other alphabet symbols can appear. This two-direction argument proves equality with {a,b}*, rather than merely showing a few example strings are generated. The ε production explicitly includes the empty word.

# GATE 2016 CS1: Q27 (printed CS Q17)

**Question:** [Official archived paper page 9](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1popAHO-cX69oQEx_tD0wZXL1tTrBljeO/view); consult original wording, diagrams and choices.

**Type / marks:** MCQ, 1 mark(s).

**Official answer:** C

**Derived answer:** C

**Source access:** Open archive member CS/CS2016.pdf inside the linked official CS.zip. Page numbers refer to the extracted PDF, not the Drive preview.

**Paraphrased problem context:** Which decision problems are undecidable? I: Given NFAs N1,N2, is L(N1) intersection L(N2) empty? II: Given CFG G and string x, is x in L(G)? III: Given CFGs G1,G2, are their languages equal? IV: Given Turing machine M, is L(M) empty? A: I,IV. B: II,III. C: III,IV. D: II,IV.

## Solution

NFA intersection emptiness is decidable by product-automaton reachability. CFG membership is decidable by parsing. Equivalence of arbitrary CFGs is undecidable, and TM-language emptiness is a nontrivial semantic property covered by Rice’s theorem. Thus III and IV, C.

For I, the product automaton accepts exactly the intersection, and finite graph search checks whether an accepting state is reachable. For II, a finite input can be handled by a terminating CFG parsing algorithm. Neither argument extends to III: comparing all words of two arbitrary CFGs is an undecidable equivalence problem. For IV, empty-language and nonempty-language Turing machines both exist, making emptiness a nontrivial property of recognized languages and hence undecidable by Rice's theorem.

# GATE 2016 CS1: Q28 (printed CS Q18)

**Question:** [Official archived paper page 9](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1popAHO-cX69oQEx_tD0wZXL1tTrBljeO/view); consult original wording, diagrams and choices.

**Type / marks:** MCQ, 1 mark(s).

**Official answer:** B

**Derived answer:** B

**Source access:** Open archive member CS/CS2016.pdf inside the linked official CS.zip. Page numbers refer to the extracted PDF, not the Drive preview.

**Paraphrased problem context:** Let Σ={0,1}; + denotes union and * Kleene star. Which regex specifies strings containing both 00 and 11 as substrings? A: Σ*0011Σ*+Σ*1100Σ*. B: Σ*(00Σ*11+11Σ*00)Σ*. C: Σ*00Σ*+Σ*11Σ*. D:00Σ*11+11Σ*00.

## Solution

A word must contain both a 00 occurrence and a 11 occurrence, in either order, with an arbitrary middle substring and arbitrary prefix/suffix. They cannot overlap because their symbols differ. Hence Σ*(00Σ*11+11Σ*00)Σ*, B. A forces adjacent blocks, C requires only one, and D disallows arbitrary outside context.

Take the earlier of a 00 occurrence and a 11 occurrence. Their positions cannot overlap, so one appears before the other with some possibly empty substring between them. This establishes the two alternatives in B. As a diagnostic example,001011 has both required pairs separated by 10, so it is valid but A rejects it. C incorrectly accepts 00 alone; D rejects valid words with extra prefix or suffix. Arbitrary prefix, middle and suffix are all needed.

# GATE 2016 CS1: Q52 (printed CS Q42)

**Question:** [Official archived paper page 16](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1popAHO-cX69oQEx_tD0wZXL1tTrBljeO/view); consult original wording, diagrams and choices.

**Type / marks:** MCQ, 2 mark(s).

**Official answer:** D

**Derived answer:** D

**Source access:** Open archive member CS/CS2016.pdf inside the linked official CS.zip. Page numbers refer to the extracted PDF, not the Drive preview.

**Paraphrased problem context:** Consider grammars G1:S→aS|B, B→b|bB; and G2:S→aA|bB, A→aA|B|ε, B→bB|ε. All options describe languages {a^m b^n} with nonnegative integer exponents. Which pair of constraints corresponds to G1,G2 respectively? A:(m>0 or n>0),(m>0 and n>0). B:(m>0 and n>0),(m>0 or n≥0). C:(m≥0 or n>0),(m>0 and n>0). D:(m≥0 and n>0),(m>0 or n>0).

## Solution

G1 emits any number of initial a symbols, then at least one b, so its language is a^m b^n with m≥0, n>0. G2 chooses an initial a or b, then permits all remaining a symbols before its b symbols; it generates every nonempty a^m b^n and not epsilon. Thus m>0 or n>0, giving D.

In G1 the only way to eliminate S is to enter B, and B has no ε rule, so a b is compulsory. In G2 the first production emits a or b, ruling out ε; after that, ε rules allow stopping. Once a derivation enters B, it emits only b symbols, so neither grammar can place an a after a b. Witnesses distinguish boundaries: b is in both languages, a is in G2 only, and ε is in neither. These tests select the inequalities in D.

# GATE 2016 CS1: Q53 (printed CS Q43)

**Question:** [Official archived paper page 17](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1popAHO-cX69oQEx_tD0wZXL1tTrBljeO/view); consult original wording, diagrams and choices.

**Type / marks:** MCQ, 2 mark(s).

**Official answer:** D

**Derived answer:** D

**Source access:** Open archive member CS/CS2016.pdf inside the linked official CS.zip. Page numbers refer to the extracted PDF, not the Drive preview.

**Paraphrased problem context:** A PDA over input {a,b}, stack {X,Z}, starts with stack Z. Its start state q0 and state q2 are accepting; q1 is not. q0 loops on a,X/XX and a,Z/XZ; q0→q1 is b,X/ε; q1 loops on b,X/ε; q1→q2 is ε,Z/Z. There are no other transitions. Acceptance is by final state after consuming the whole input. Which statement is true? A:L={a^n b^n:n≥0}, not finite-automaton recognizable. B:L=a* union {a^n b^n:n≥0}, not accepted by any deterministic PDA. C:L is not accepted by any Turing machine halting on all inputs. D:L=a* union {a^n b^n:n≥0}, and is deterministic context-free.

## Solution

The initial state is accepting, so epsilon and every a-only word are accepted while pushing one X per a. On the first b the machine moves to the middle state and pops one X per b; it reaches the final accepting state only when the stack returns to Z. Therefore the additional accepted words are a^n b^n. The displayed machine is deterministic: at each state/stack combination the input transitions do not compete with epsilon transitions. The language is a* union {a^n b^n: n≥0}, a deterministic CFL, D.

Final-state acceptance does not require an empty stack. This is why an all-a input is accepted in q0 even with X symbols left above Z, and why the double circle on the start state matters. Once a b occurs the machine cannot return to q0 or read further a symbols. It can reach q2 exactly after the number of b symbols matches the pushed X count. At q1, b-transitions require top X whereas the ε-transition requires top Z, so they are never simultaneously enabled; determinism is preserved.

# GATE 2016 CS1: Q54 (printed CS Q44)

**Question:** [Official archived paper page 17](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1popAHO-cX69oQEx_tD0wZXL1tTrBljeO/view); consult original wording, diagrams and choices.

**Type / marks:** MCQ, 2 mark(s).

**Official answer:** C

**Derived answer:** C

**Source access:** Open archive member CS/CS2016.pdf inside the linked official CS.zip. Page numbers refer to the extracted PDF, not the Drive preview.

**Paraphrased problem context:** X is recursive; Y is recursively enumerable but not recursive. There are computable many-one reductions complement(Y)≤m W and Z≤m complement(X). Which conclusion is correct? A:W can be recursively enumerable and Z is recursive. B:W can be recursive and Z is recursively enumerable. C:W is not recursively enumerable and Z is recursive. D:W is not recursively enumerable and Z is not recursive. The complement bars are part of the printed source, although plain PDF extraction omits them.

## Solution

The source has complement bars: complement(Y) reduces to W, and Z reduces to complement(X). Since Y is RE but not recursive, complement(Y) cannot be RE, otherwise dovetailing the two recognizers would decide Y. RE languages are closed under computable many-one preimages, so W cannot be RE. X recursive implies complement(X) recursive, and its computable preimage Z is recursive. Hence C. The complement bars were visually checked; text extraction omits them.

The direction of the reduction is crucial. To recognize complement(Y) from a recognizer for W, compute the reduction image and run that recognizer. Thus if W were RE, complement(Y) would be RE, contradicting the fact that an RE language with an RE complement is decidable. For Z, compute its reduction image and run the decider for complement(X), which halts on all inputs. This closure argument proves Z recursive without assuming anything about its syntax or structure.

# GATE 2016 CS2: Q26 (printed CS Q16)

**Question:** [Official archived paper page 29](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1popAHO-cX69oQEx_tD0wZXL1tTrBljeO/view); consult original wording, diagrams and choices.

**Type / marks:** NAT, 1 mark(s).

**Official answer:** 2.0 : 2.0

**Derived answer:** 2

**Source access:** Open archive member CS/CS2016.pdf inside the linked official CS.zip. Page numbers refer to the extracted PDF, not the Drive preview.

**Paraphrased problem context:** How many states does a minimum DFA need for (0+1)*(0+1)(0+1)*, where + denotes union?

## Solution

The expression Σ*ΣΣ* is exactly the nonempty binary strings. Use a nonaccepting start state and one accepting state reached by either symbol, with both loops on the latter. The empty string differs from every nonempty word, so at least two states are necessary.

The mandatory middle (0+1) contributes at least one symbol, while the starred parts may be empty. The transition table is start:0→accept,1→accept; accept:0→accept,1→accept. The empty suffix distinguishes start from accept because only one is accepting, establishing minimality rather than merely constructing a two-state automaton.

# GATE 2016 CS2: Q27 (printed CS Q17)

**Question:** [Official archived paper page 29](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1popAHO-cX69oQEx_tD0wZXL1tTrBljeO/view); consult original wording, diagrams and choices.

**Type / marks:** MCQ, 1 mark(s).

**Official answer:** C

**Derived answer:** C

**Source access:** Open archive member CS/CS2016.pdf inside the linked official CS.zip. Page numbers refer to the extracted PDF, not the Drive preview.

**Paraphrased problem context:** L1 has grammar S1→aS1b|ε, and L2 has S2→abS2|ε. P: L1 is regular; Q: L2 is regular. A both; B P only; C Q only; D neither.

## Solution

L1={a^n b^n: n≥0}, nonregular by pumping/distinguishable prefixes. L2=(ab)* is regular. Therefore P false, Q true, C.

Each use of S1→aS1b adds one a and one b at opposite ends; ε stops the derivation. Pumping an a-prefix of a^p b^p changes only the a count, proving nonregularity. In contrast, S2 repeatedly appends the fixed block ab; a three-state complete DFA can check alternating a,b blocks and reject violations.

# GATE 2016 CS2: Q28 (printed CS Q18)

**Question:** [Official archived paper page 30](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1popAHO-cX69oQEx_tD0wZXL1tTrBljeO/view); consult original wording, diagrams and choices.

**Type / marks:** MCQ, 1 mark(s).

**Official answer:** D

**Derived answer:** D

**Source access:** Open archive member CS/CS2016.pdf inside the linked official CS.zip. Page numbers refer to the extracted PDF, not the Drive preview.

**Paraphrased problem context:** L1 is regular, L2 context-free, L3 recursive and L4 recursively enumerable. Which are always true? I ¬L3∪L4 is RE; II ¬L2∪L3 is recursive; III L1*∩L2 is context-free; IV L1∪¬L2 is context-free. Complements use the common alphabet-star. A I only; B I,III; C I,IV; D I,II,III.

## Solution

The source complement bars matter. I: complement(L3) is recursive and its union with RE L4 is RE. II: every CFL is recursive, so complement(L2) and its union with recursive L3 are recursive. III: L1* is regular and its intersection with a CFL is CFL. IV is not guaranteed because taking L1 empty leaves complement(L2), and CFLs are not closed under complement. Thus I, II, III, D.

Do not confuse “not context-free” with “undecidable.” Every CFL has a terminating membership algorithm, so its complement is decidable even though it may cease to be context-free. For III, run a finite automaton for L1* alongside a pushdown automaton for L2. The finite control adds no second stack, preserving context-freeness.

# GATE 2016 CS2: Q52 (printed CS Q42)

**Question:** [Official archived paper page 37](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1popAHO-cX69oQEx_tD0wZXL1tTrBljeO/view); consult original wording, diagrams and choices.

**Type / marks:** MCQ, 2 mark(s).

**Official answer:** B

**Derived answer:** B

**Source access:** Open archive member CS/CS2016.pdf inside the linked official CS.zip. Page numbers refer to the extracted PDF, not the Drive preview.

**Paraphrased problem context:** I: If all NFA states accept, its language is Σ*. II: There exists a regular language A for which A∩B is regular for every language B. A I only; B II only; C both; D neither.

## Solution

An NFA can have missing transitions. One accepting start state with no transitions accepts only epsilon, not Σ* for a nonempty alphabet, disproving I. For II choose the regular language A=empty set; its intersection with every B is empty and hence regular. Thus only II, B.

Acceptance by an NFA requires at least one complete run consuming the entire word. An accepting state alone cannot consume an unavailable transition; for the one-state counterexample any nonempty word has no run. II is existential in A but universal in B, so choosing a fixed empty A handles even nonregular or undecidable B at once.

# GATE 2016 CS2: Q53 (printed CS Q43)

**Question:** [Official archived paper page 37](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1popAHO-cX69oQEx_tD0wZXL1tTrBljeO/view); consult original wording, diagrams and choices.

**Type / marks:** MCQ, 2 mark(s).

**Official answer:** B

**Derived answer:** B

**Source access:** Open archive member CS/CS2016.pdf inside the linked official CS.zip. Page numbers refer to the extracted PDF, not the Drive preview.

**Paraphrased problem context:** L1={a^n b^m c^(n+m):m,n≥1}; L2={a^n b^n c^(2n):n≥1}. A both context-free; B only L1; C only L2; D neither.

## Solution

L1 is generated by S→aSc|aBc and B→bBc|bc: each a or b adds one trailing c, with positive counts of both. Thus L1 is context-free. If L2 were context-free, its inverse image under h(a)=a, h(b)=b, h(c)=cc would be {a^n b^n c^n: n≥1}, which is not context-free by the pumping lemma. CFL closure under inverse homomorphism therefore proves L2 non-context-free. Answer B.

A pushdown intuition for L1 pushes one marker per a or b and pops one per c, with finite control enforcing the a-then-b-then-c phases. L2 must enforce three linked quantities. Under h(c)=cc, an input a^n b^n c^n maps exactly to a^n b^n c^(2n), transferring the known non-CFL obstruction through inverse homomorphism.

# GATE 2016 CS2: Q54 (printed CS Q44)

**Question:** [Official archived paper page 38](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1popAHO-cX69oQEx_tD0wZXL1tTrBljeO/view); consult original wording, diagrams and choices.

**Type / marks:** MCQ, 2 mark(s).

**Official answer:** C

**Derived answer:** C

**Source access:** Open archive member CS/CS2016.pdf inside the linked official CS.zip. Page numbers refer to the extracted PDF, not the Drive preview.

**Paraphrased problem context:** Let L1={⟨M⟩:M takes at least 2016 steps on some input}, L2={⟨M⟩:M takes at least 2016 steps on all inputs}, L3={⟨M⟩:M accepts ε}. Which are recursive? A only L1; B only L2; C L1 and L2 only; D all three.

## Solution

Whether a machine takes at least2016 steps depends only on its first 2016-step computation prefix. In that time its input head can inspect only a bounded initial segment, so finitely many representative inputs suffice: all short inputs and one representative extension for each sufficiently long prefix. Simulate each for the fixed bound and test whether any (L1) or every (L2) representative survives that many steps. Both tests halt. Acceptance of epsilon (L3) is undecidable by the standard reduction that builds a machine ignoring its input and simulating an arbitrary machine/input pair. Hence C.

The constant 2016 is essential: this is bounded simulation, not the general halting problem. A machine cannot inspect arbitrarily far into its input in a fixed number of steps. For L3, given M,w, construct N that ignores its own input and simulates M on w, accepting iff M accepts w. Deciding whether N accepts ε would decide the undecidable acceptance problem.
